question: According to recent media reports1, the Czech authorities detained and subsequently expelled two Russian nationals linked to Russian propaganda structures. One of them, Vitaliy Chashchukhin, reportedly resides legally in Germany and works for Russian media outlets, including Izvestia and REN TV, whose broadcasting activities in the EU are subject to EU restrictive measures.
Despite being expelled from Czechia, he was reportedly able to return to Germany, from where he has been operating and travelling within the Schengen area. 1.
Is the Commission aware that individuals working for Russian media outlets subject to EU restrictive measures are legally residing in and operating from Member States, including Germany?
How does the Commission assess the enforcement of EU sanctions in cases where individuals provide services to sanctioned Russian media while residing in the EU?

Does the Commission consider the current coordination and information exchange between the Member States sufficient to prevent the EU and the Schengen area from being used as a base for Russian propaganda operations?
Seznam Zprávy, https://www.seznamzpravy.cz/clanek/domaci-kauzy-ceska-policie-vykazala-ruskepropagandisty-vyslychala-je-pry-devet-hodin-315493. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The Commission is aware of sanctions circumvention tactics by individuals linked to Russian state‑controlled media. The Commission does not comment on single cases, in particular while national enforcement actions are ongoing.

The Commission recalls that Council Regulation (EU) No 833/20141 suspends the broadcasting in the EU of content from certain media outlets, which are sanctioned for their role in promoting and propagandising Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine. EU persons are banned from enabling, facilitating or otherwise contributing to the broadcasting of such content.

Moreover, the EU has also imposed sanctions on individuals and entities who engage in actions undermining the stability of third countries, including information manipulation and interference. Sanctioned individuals are subject to a travel ban.

Member States are responsible for investigations, enforcement and the application of penalties when EU sanctions are violated, in line also with their obligations under Directive (EU) 2024/12262. Issues of sanctions implementation and circumvention are followed closely by Commission services, including through regular information exchange with national competent authorities.

Member States remain responsible for the decisions on entry, stay and return of third country nationals, and for maintaining a high level of security in the Schengen area. Tools to support information exchange and operational cooperation between Member States, such as the Schengen Information System (SIS), are in place and actively used.
1 Article 2f, Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of

Russia's actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A02014R0833-20260724. 2 Directive (EU) 2024/1226 of 24 April 2024 on the definition of criminal offences and penalties for the violation of Union restrictive measures: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1226/oj/eng.
